summary: This informational memo gives a framework for Layer 3 provider-provisioned VPNs. It aims to help standardise protocols and mechanisms by describing the significant components in a coherent way.

eli5.summary: There are many ways to build a private network over someone else's network. This document draws the big picture so the pieces fit.

subtitle: A map of the design choices for Layer 3 VPNs run by a service provider: who routes, how sites find each other, and how traffic is tunneled.

tldr.problem: Service providers can build Layer 3 VPNs for customers in many different ways, and standards need a common vocabulary and a clear list of the technical issues.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC gives reference models for PE-based and provider-provisioned CE-based VPNs. It then walks through the customer interface, VPN discovery, tunneling, routing distribution, QoS, management, interworking and security, describing several options for each without choosing one.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational framework, not a protocol. Picking approaches and writing protocol details is left to other documents.

today: RFC 4110 is an Informational framework and has not been obsoleted or updated. It names its requirements companions as RFC 3809 and RFC 4031.

sections.title: What a Layer 3 PPVPN Is
sections.content:
A Virtual Private Network (VPN) is a set of sites that can talk to each other, with restricted communication to outsiders, over a network infrastructure shared with sites that are not in the VPN. That shared infrastructure is the VPN backbone. A provider-provisioned VPN (PPVPN) is one the service provider helps manage and provision. This framework covers Layer 3 VPNs over an IP and/or MPLS backbone, where the provider's edge devices decide how to route VPN traffic by looking at IP and/or MPLS headers.

Customer networks often use private addresses (RFC 1918) that can overlap between customers, so packets cannot cross the provider network in native form. Some form of encapsulation or tunneling must be used. VPNs can be intranets (one customer administration) or extranets (several).

The RFC takes a "horizontal" approach: for each issue it describes several approaches and makes no choice. Specific solutions are "vertical" and live in other documents.
sections.eli5: A VPN is a private club that meets using the same roads as everyone else. Because club members might use the same street names as other clubs, their traffic rides in sealed envelopes.

sections.title: Reference Models and Roles
sections.content:
The RFC distinguishes two kinds of Layer 3 VPN. In a CE-based VPN, the provider edge (PE) devices know nothing about the customer's routing or addressing, and the tunnels run between customer edge (CE) devices; the provider just manages those CE devices. In a PE-based VPN, tunnels end at the PE devices, which route customer packets by their IP addresses, so CE devices need no special VPN capability.

In PE-based VPNs each PE keeps a separate VPN Forwarding Instance (VFI) per VPN: the routing and forwarding information for that VPN. P routers in the core hold no VPN state and have no direct attachment to CE devices. A CE can be multi-homed to more than one PE for robustness, and the RFC shows four such arrangements.

Because different providers may choose different approaches, the RFC also describes three ways to interwork: an interworking function (a PE sitting between two approaches), an interworking interface (per-VPN tunnels between PEs of different approaches, handled like a CE-to-PE link), and customer-based interworking, where a customer site simply attaches to both kinds.
sections.eli5: Either the customer's own door-keeper (CE) packs the sealed envelopes, or the road company's door-keeper (PE) does it. Each road-company door-keeper keeps a separate address book for each club.

sections.title: Routing Between Customer and Provider
sections.content:
For PE-based VPNs, the PE and CE can exchange routes using static routing, an IGP such as RIP, OSPF or IS-IS, or BGP. A PE learns the addresses reachable through a CE and passes them to the other PEs of the same VPN, which pass them on to their CEs. VPN routing information is never distributed to P routers. In a CE-based VPN, the PE and CE do not exchange the customer's routes; sites can instead exchange them over the CE-CE tunnels, or the provider's management system can configure static routes.

Between PEs, the RFC describes two models. Per-VPN routing runs a separate routing instance for each VPN, so each PE behaves like several independent routers, at the cost of many adjacencies. The aggregated routing model carries all VPN routes in one routing protocol. Aggregating with OSPF or IS-IS does not work well because link-state flooding gives every PE the same information. BGP can constrain distribution with filters and route reflectors, and VPN routes are kept distinct from public routes, for example with separate address families.

Scaling is a recurring theme. The RFC works an example of 1000 VPNs with an average of 100 sites each and 10 prefixes per site, which would need about 1,000,000 VPN prefixes on a PE, and suggests keeping the PE's Internet routing to a default route.
sections.eli5: Each door-keeper tells the others which addresses live behind their door. Using one big shared notice board is neater than one board per club, but you must make sure each person only reads the notices meant for them.

sections.title: Discovery, Topology and Management
sections.content:
Any VPN solution has three logical stages: VPN edge devices learn of each other (discovery), they establish tunnels, and they exchange routing information. Not every solution separates these stages cleanly. Membership information can come from a network management system, from a directory server (LDAPv3 is mentioned), or be piggybacked on BGP, where an update says a PE joined a VPN and a withdraw says it left. Manual configuration is discouraged because it does not scale and is error prone.

VPN topology is an administrative choice: a full mesh, hub and spoke, or arbitrary. A full mesh of N edge devices needs N*(N-1)/2 duplex tunnels, which is one reason for partial meshes. A hub and spoke layout fits, for example, many telecommuters reaching a few corporate sites, and can force traffic through a firewall.

The RFC also covers QoS using IntServ/RSVP and DiffServ, concurrent access to a VPN and the Internet (which needs NAT and traffic analysis such as a firewall), and network and customer management, where it prefers standard interfaces such as SNMP, XML or LDAP and per-VPN segregation of management information.
sections.eli5: First the door-keepers must find each other, then dig tunnels, then swap address lists. The club decides whether everyone connects directly or through a central hub.

sections.title: Tunneling Options
sections.content:
Tunnels carry VPN packets across the backbone. When a tunnel packet arrives, the egress must work out which VPN it belongs to from a multiplexing field. The RFC surveys four techniques:

  • GRE (RFC 2784, RFC 2890): the Key field can serve for multiplexing. At least 28 bytes of overhead over IPv4, 36 with the key.
  • IP-in-IP (RFC 2003, RFC 2473): no real multiplexing field, so each VPN needs a different destination IP address. At least 20 bytes.
  • IPsec: the SPI field multiplexes security associations. At least 8 bytes in transport mode and at least 28 bytes in tunnel mode, and it offers authentication, integrity and optional privacy.
  • MPLS (RFC 3031): the label stack identifies the VPN. 4 bytes per label, the lightest overhead, but it cannot be guaranteed to run over any IP network.

GRE, IP-in-IP and MPLS provide no significant security by themselves. To keep core state small, the RFC recommends hierarchical tunnels: one outer tunnel per pair of edge devices carrying many per-VPN tunnels, so state depends on the number of edge devices and not the number of VPNs. The appendix adds optimizations, such as penultimate hop popping, to reduce header lookups.
sections.eli5: There are four kinds of sealed envelopes. Some are thick, some thin, and each has a different way of writing which club the letter belongs to. Putting many club letters into one big envelope between two door-keepers saves the roads from tracking every club.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC treats security as a key requirement and walks through system security, access control, endpoint authentication, data integrity and confidentiality. In PE-based VPNs the provider is responsible for confidentiality, using separation through VFIs and tunnels; where a tunnel crosses untrusted networks, stronger measures such as encryption are needed. In CE-based VPNs the CE enforces authentication, integrity and confidentiality, for example with IPsec. Both user data and VPN control data must be protected to prevent deliberate misconfiguration, and inter-SP VPNs add the risk of conflicting configuration between providers.
sections.eli5: The road company must lock its own buildings and keep clubs separate. If the envelopes travel over roads it does not control, it should also scramble the letters.
